extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers of science, and graduate students interested in theory choice and the philosophy of scientific practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and choosing between competing scientific theories, focusing on the values, exemplars, and cognitive processes that underlie theory acceptance and scientific revolutions. Emphasizes predictive performance, simplicity, consistency, exemplars/tacit knowledge, persuasion, and incommensurability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive accuracy (including precision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Predictions should be accurate; quantitative predictions are preferable to qualitative ones; whatever the margin of permissible error, it should be consistently satisfied in a given field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the text: 'Probably the most deeply held values concern predictions: they should be accurate; quantitative predictions are preferable to qualitative ones; whatever the margin of permissible error, it should be consistently satisfied in a given field.' Use predictive success and reliable precision as a central criterion when judging theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit puzzle-formulation and solution
rubrics_metrics.description: A good theory must permit puzzle-formulation and solution: it should enable the identification and resolution of scientific puzzles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author lists this as 'first and foremost' among values for judging whole theories: theories must permit puzzle-formulation and solution. In practice, evaluate whether a theory generates solvable problems and productive puzzles for normal science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, theories should be simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity is a valued attribute to be applied when comparing theories, but its application can vary among individuals and groups; it functions as a value rather than a strict rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-consistency (internal consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories should be self-consistent (internally coherent) across their statements and derivations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal consistency is named among the values to judge theories; the author notes that insufficient attention to internal/external consistency was a weakness in earlier text—thus emphasize consistency when diagnosing crises or choosing theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories should be plausible — i.e., they should present a credible account compatible with scientists' judgments about what is reasonable or believable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plausibility is listed alongside simplicity and consistency; it is a value applied variably by individuals and communities and contributes to theory acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with other currently deployed theories (external consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories should, where possible, be compatible with other theories currently deployed in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compatibility is mentioned as a desideratum for whole theories; assess how well a candidate theory integrates with the body of accepted theory, or whether it requires costly revision of widely used frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of exemplars / shared concrete problem-solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Shared exemplars — concrete problem-solutions encountered in training and literature — are central components that illustrate how theories are applied and provide the fine-structure of a scientific community's practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes exemplars (examples like inclined plane, conical pendulum, Keplerian orbits) as essential for learning, for providing empirical content to laws, and for shaping how practitioners 'see' problems. When evaluating work, check whether relevant exemplars are used to ground claims and training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical content via exemplars rather than abstract rules alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical content of laws/theories often arises only when accompanied by concrete exemplars; verbal statements of laws alone may be 'virtually impotent' without exemplars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a theory or explanation is tied to concrete examples that show how terms/functionings map to observations. Beware of relying solely on abstract verbal formulation without demonstrative problem-solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tacit knowledge and learning-by-doing
rubrics_metrics.description: Important knowledge is tacit, learned through practice with exemplars and not fully expressible as explicit rules or criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that knowledge embedded in exemplars is 'tacit' and acquired through doing; peer review should recognize demonstration of tacit competencies (e.g., skillful problem-solving, intuitive identification) as legitimate evidence of understanding even if not fully formalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquired similarity relations / gestalt recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists acquire ways of seeing situations as similar (gestalt-like recognition) through repeated exemplar experience, enabling them to design appropriate law-sketches for new problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether practitioners demonstrate the ability to map new problems to known exemplars and to construct or adapt law-sketches; this capacity is central to competency but may not be captured by explicit criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for perception vs interpretation distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception (trained, often involuntary recognition) and interpretation (deliberative application of criteria) are different processes; scientific competence includes both appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing work, distinguish between what is presented as immediate perceptual recognition (expert 'seeing') and what is offered as interpretative argument; both have roles, but conflating them (treating perception as unconscious interpretation via rules) is a mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgement of incommensurability and partial communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Debates between proponents of competing theories often involve parties who 'see' certain experimental situations differently and may attach the same terms to nature differently, producing only partial communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review and theory-assessment should recognize that proponents may genuinely disagree about what observations mean; arguments should aim at persuasion and conversion rather than assuming a neutral algorithm will decide the matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasion and community decision-making (no neutral algorithm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory choice in debates cannot be cast fully as logical proof; parties must persuade others because there is no neutral algorithmic decision procedure guaranteeing identical choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values (accuracy, simplicity, fruitfulness, scope) function as criteria but are applied variably; reviewers should judge both the reasons offered and their persuasive power within the specialist community, acknowledging the community's role in the effective decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Values function as evaluative criteria but are applied variably
rubrics_metrics.description: Values such as accuracy, simplicity, and fruitfulness are used to judge theories, but different individuals may weigh them differently leading to different choices without being irrational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluation, make explicit which values are being applied and justify their relative weight. Recognize that differing weighings are not necessarily mistakes, and that community-level convergence often results from shared values interacting with shared experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of risk through shared values and tolerance of individual variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Communities rely on shared values rather than strict rules to distribute risk: individual variability in applying values can be essential to scientific progress (some resist, some take risks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a scientific community's practices allow both conservative and high-risk routes; value systems that channel diverse individual responses can foster both normal science and revolutionary change. An anti-pattern is demanding uniform application of values that would stifle necessary diversity of response.
